questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on the forearm with a raised indurated border and central black eschar after handling animal hides. Gram stain reveals large gram-positive rods in chains. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 60 days
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 60 days
Penicillin V 500 mg four times daily for 7 days
Clindamycin 300 mg three times daily for 14 days
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) is treated with ciprofloxacin or doxycycline for 60 days. Doxycycline is the drug of choice when bioterrorism is not suspected. For mass casualty events, ciprofloxacin is preferred.

questions.q: A 28-year-old immunocompetent woman presents with painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the right T5 dermatome. She reports prodromal pain for 2 days. Which antiviral should be started?
opts: Acyclovir 200 mg 5 times daily for 5 days
Valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days
Famciclovir 250 mg three times daily for 7 days
Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days
questions.exp: Herpes zoster is treated with acyclovir 800 mg 5 times/day for 7 days or valacyclovir 1 g TID for 7 days or famciclovir 500 mg TID for 7 days. Valacyclovir and famciclovir have better bioavailability. The option listing famciclovir 250 mg is incorrect dosing (should be 500 mg). Acyclovir 800 mg 5x/day for 7 days is correct.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with a painless genital ulcer with a clean base and indurated edges. VDRL is non-reactive. Dark field microscopy of the ulcer exudate shows motile spirochetes. What is the diagnosis and treatment of choice?
opts: Primary syphilis — Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
LGV — Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days
Granuloma inguinale — Azithromycin 1 g weekly for 3 weeks
questions.exp: The painless indurated ulcer with positive dark-field microscopy for Treponema pallidum confirms primary syphilis. VDRL can be non-reactive early. Treatment is benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on multidrug therapy develops sudden onset of painful erythematous nodules over the face and extremities with fever and malaise. Nerve tenderness is absent. What is this reaction and its management?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL/Type 2 reaction) occurs in BL and LL leprosy. It is immune complex mediated (Type III hypersensitivity). Thalidomide is the most effective treatment (100-400 mg/day) but is contraindicated in women of childbearing age. Clofazimine and prednisolone are alternatives.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman develops tense bullae on normal-appearing and erythematous skin, predominantly on the flexures and trunk. Nikolsky sign is negative. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense bullae, negative Nikolsky sign, and linear IgG/C3 at the DEJ on DIF. It targets BP180 and BP230 antigens in the hemidesmosomes. Pemphigus vulgaris shows intraepidermal split and IgG in a 'chicken-wire' pattern on DIF.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman with malar rash, oral ulcers, and arthritis has ANA positive at 1:640 with anti-dsDNA positive. She develops discoid lesions on sun-exposed areas. Which skin finding is most specific for SLE?
questions.exp: Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) lesions with follicular plugging, scarring, and hypopigmentation are highly specific for lupus. Malar rash is sensitive but less specific. DLE occurring in SLE indicates chronic cutaneous lupus.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male smoker presents with a pearly papule with telangiectasias and a rolled border on the nose. It has been slowly growing for 2 years. Dermoscopy shows arborising vessels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (nodular type) classically presents as a pearly papule with telangiectasias, rolled border, and arborising (tree-like) vessels on dermoscopy. It is the most common skin cancer. Sun-exposed areas of the head and neck are most affected.

questions.q: A 40-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with multiple soft, skin-colored papules with central umbilication on the face. CD4 count is 80 cells/µL. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum caused by MCV (a poxvirus) presents with umbilicated papules. In HIV patients with CD4 <200, it can be widespread and giant (>5mm). Facial involvement is a marker of advanced immunosuppression. Treatment with HAART leads to resolution.

questions.q: During a Wood's lamp examination of a patient with tinea capitis, you observe bright green fluorescence. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Microsporum canis produces ectothrix infection with bright green (yellow-green) fluorescence under Wood's lamp. T. tonsurans and T. violaceum (endothrix fungi) do not fluoresce. T. schoenleinii produces pale green fluorescence in favus.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches on the trunk, with loss of sweating in the patches. Slit skin smear is negative. Skin biopsy shows granulomas around dermal nerves. What type of leprosy does this represent?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) shows well-defined hypopigmented anaesthetic patches with loss of sweating and hair. Biopsy shows epithelioid granulomas invading and destroying dermal nerves. Slit skin smear is negative (paucibacillary). Cell-mediated immunity is high.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with painful genital ulcers, unilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy, and a groove sign (inguinal and femoral lymphadenopathy separated by Poupart's ligament). Complement fixation test is positive at >1:64. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: LGV (Chlamydia trachomatis L1-L3) characteristically causes the 'groove sign' — a groove between the inguinal and femoral nodes separated by Poupart's ligament. The complement fixation test >1:64 supports LGV. Treatment is doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days.

questions.q: A patient on dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis develops sudden onset cyanosis, chocolate-brown blood, and dyspnea. Pulse oximetry shows 85% but ABG shows normal PaO2. What is the likely complication?
questions.exp: Methemoglobinemia is a dose-dependent adverse effect of dapsone. Classic features: cyanosis not responding to O2, chocolate-brown blood, normal PaO2 on ABG (since ABG measures dissolved O2, not oxygen saturation). Treatment: methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV.

questions.q: A 20-year-old presents with flesh-colored to pink grouped papules in the axillae and neck. Histology shows acanthosis, papillomatosis, and hyperkeratosis with horn-cyst formation. The lesion shows a 'church spire' pattern. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Seborrheic keratosis histology shows acanthosis, papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, horn cysts, and a characteristic 'church spire' pattern of exophytic papillomatous projections. It is the most common benign skin tumour in older adults, but can appear earlier.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops palpable purpura on the lower legs, arthralgias, and peripheral neuropathy. Cryoglobulins are detected. Which type of vasculitis is this?
questions.exp: Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis presents with the classic triad of purpura, arthralgia, and weakness/neuropathy, with detectable cryoglobulins. It is associated with HCV infection, lymphoma, and autoimmune diseases. DIF shows IgM, IgG, and C3 in vessel walls.

questions.q: A 16-year-old presents with comedones, inflammatory papules, and nodules on the face and back. His acne has not responded to 3 months of oral antibiotics. What is the drug of choice for severe nodulo-cystic acne?
questions.exp: Oral isotretinoin (0.5-1 mg/kg/day) for 15-20 weeks is the drug of choice for severe nodulo-cystic acne and acne unresponsive to antibiotics. It targets all four pathogenic factors: sebum production, follicular keratinization, P. acnes, and inflammation.

questions.q: A 35-year-old presents with depigmented patches on the face and hands since childhood. The patches show complete loss of pigment with hyperpigmented borders. Wood's lamp shows chalky-white fluorescence. Family history is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Vitiligo presents with chalk-white macules accentuated under Wood's lamp. The hyperpigmented border (trichrome vitiligo) and positive family history support the diagnosis. Melanocytes are absent in established lesions. It is autoimmune in pathogenesis.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman on hydroxyurea for polycythemia vera develops painful leg ulcers, skin hyperpigmentation, and longitudinal melanonychia. She has been on the drug for 5 years. What nail change is characteristic of hydroxyurea toxicity?
questions.exp: Hydroxyurea causes longitudinal melanonychia (brown-black longitudinal bands), leg ulcers, skin hyperpigmentation, and dermatomyositis-like changes. These are cutaneous side effects of long-term use. Beau's lines indicate systemic illness; Mees' lines occur with arsenic poisoning.

questions.q: A biopsy from a bullous lesion shows suprabasal acantholysis with 'tombstone' appearance of the basal layer. DIF shows IgG in a 'fish-net' pattern throughout the epidermis. What is the target antigen?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris (mucosal-dominant) targets desmoglein 3 (DSG3). Suprabasal acantholysis with tombstoning and IgG in epidermal intercellular spaces on DIF are characteristic. Desmoglein 1 is targeted in pemphigus foliaceus (subcorneal split). BP180 and collagen VII are targeted in subepidermal blistering disorders.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male presents with proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules over the knuckles, and periungual erythema. CK is markedly elevated. What autoantibody is associated with interstitial lung disease in this condition?
questions.exp: Anti-Jo-1 (anti-tRNA synthetase) antibody is associated with the antisynthetase syndrome: inflammatory myopathy + ILD + mechanic's hands + arthritis + Raynaud's. Anti-Mi-2 is associated with classic dermatomyositis (good prognosis). Anti-MDA5 is associated with amyopathic DM and rapidly progressive ILD.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with scaly plaques in the groin and inner thighs. KOH mount shows hyphae with terminal and intercalary chlamydoconidia. The macroconidia are thin-walled, smooth, and cigar-shaped. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Epidermophyton floccosum causes tinea cruris and tinea pedis. It produces only macroconidia (no microconidia) — thin-walled, smooth, club/paddle-shaped macroconidia in clusters. T. rubrum also causes tinea cruris but has pencil-shaped macroconidia and abundant microconidia.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on dapsone develops fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and an exfoliative erythematous rash 4-6 weeks after starting therapy. CBC shows eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytes. What is this reaction?
questions.exp: Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DHS) occurs 4-6 weeks after starting dapsone. Features: fever, morbilliform/exfoliative rash, hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and atypical lymphocytosis. It is a drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS). Dapsone must be stopped immediately.

questions.q: A 30-year-old pregnant woman in the third trimester develops intensely pruritic urticarial papules and plaques in the periumbilical area, sparing the umbilicus itself, then spreading to the extremities. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP/PUPPP) characteristically begins in abdominal striae, sparing the umbilicus, in the third trimester, often in primigravidae with large weight gain/multiple gestation. It is pruritic but benign with no fetal risk. Pemphigoid gestationis starts periumbilically but forms bullae and has C3 at DEJ on DIF.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with reddish-brown plaques on the lower legs with superficial scaling, telangiectasias, and hemosiderin deposits. The plaques are indurated. He has a history of deep vein thrombosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lipodermatosclerosis (sclerosing panniculitis) results from chronic venous insufficiency. Features include indurated, hyperpigmented plaques on the lower legs with hemosiderin deposits, inverted 'champagne bottle' appearance, and history of DVT/varicosities. Treatment: compression stockings, stanozolol.

questions.q: During Mohs micrographic surgery, the surgeon performs serial horizontal frozen sections. What is the primary advantage of this technique over standard excision?
opts: Faster procedure with less operating time
Maximal tissue sparing with complete margin assessment
Better cosmetic result due to smaller incision
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery provides complete peripheral and deep margin assessment (100% of surgical margins) while maximally sparing normal tissue. Standard excision only samples 1-2% of the margin. It is the gold standard for BCC, SCC in high-risk locations, recurrent tumors, and tumors with ill-defined borders.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with painful soft chancre with undermined edges and a dirty grey base on the penis. Inguinal lymph nodes are tender, fluctuant, and may discharge through one sinus. Gram stain shows Gram-negative coccobacilli in 'school of fish' pattern. What is the treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM stat
questions.exp: Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi) presents as a painful, soft ulcer with ragged undermined edges and suppurative inguinal adenopathy (bubo). Treatment: azithromycin 1 g single dose, or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM, or erythromycin 500 mg TID for 7 days, or ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 3 days. Azithromycin single dose ensures compliance.

questions.q: A 60-year-old farmer presents with verrucous, warty plaques on the dorsum of the foot and lower leg. Direct microscopy of scales shows dematiaceous hyphae in a 'copper penny' or Medlar body pattern. What is the causative group of organisms?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis presents with verrucous plaques and characteristic muriform cells (Medlar bodies/copper pennies) — brown, thick-walled, septate cells formed by sclerotic body division. Causative agents include Fonsecaea pedrosoi (most common), Cladophialophora carrionii, Phialophora verrucosa. Treatment: itraconazole or terbinafine.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman on long-term chloroquine for discoid lupus erythematosus complains of difficulty reading. What is the mechanism of chloroquine retinopathy and which layer is primarily damaged?
opts: Corneal deposits (vortex keratopathy) damaging the corneal endothelium
Toxic damage to the retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptors (bull's eye maculopathy)
Increased intraocular pressure damaging the optic nerve
Anterior uveitis damaging the iris pigment layer
questions.exp: Chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine causes bull's eye maculopathy due to toxic damage to the retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptors in the parafoveal region. It is irreversible. Fundoscopy shows a bull's eye pattern. Recommended screening: Humphrey visual fields + OCT annually after 5 years of use or high cumulative dose.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted lesions around the mouth and nose. The mother reports the child attends daycare. Gram stain from the crust shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which organism and treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Group A Streptococcus — oral amoxicillin for 10 days
Staphylococcus aureus — topical mupirocin 2% for limited lesions
questions.exp: Bullous and non-bullous impetigo in children is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (gram-positive cocci in clusters). For limited lesions, topical mupirocin 2% TID for 5-7 days is the first-line treatment. Widespread impetigo requires oral antibiotics (cephalexin or dicloxacillin). Mupirocin reduces spread in daycare settings.

questions.q: A biopsy from a skin lesion in a patient with systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) shows increased collagen deposition in the reticular dermis, loss of adnexal structures, and a 'square biopsy sign.' What is the pathogenesis of fibrosis in this condition?
opts: TGF-β mediated fibroblast activation and excessive collagen synthesis
IL-17 mediated neutrophil infiltration with collagen degradation
TNF-α mediated macrophage activation and elastin deposition
IL-4 mediated mast cell degranulation and mucin deposition
questions.exp: Systemic sclerosis fibrosis is driven primarily by TGF-β (transforming growth factor-beta), which activates fibroblasts to differentiate into myofibroblasts and produce excessive type I and III collagen. Vascular injury, autoimmunity (anti-Scl-70, anti-centromere), and immune dysregulation also contribute. The 'square biopsy sign' reflects dermal fibrosis reaching the deep dermis.

questions.q: A 48-year-old male presents with nodular lesions on the lower extremities, face, and oral mucosa. He is HIV-positive with CD4 count of 50. Biopsy shows spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces and extravasated red blood cells. What is the causative agent?
questions.exp: AIDS-related Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8/KSHV). The biopsy shows spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. HAART leads to regression of KS. Locally, radiotherapy, cryotherapy, or intralesional vinblastine can be used; for disseminated disease, liposomal doxorubicin or paclitaxel.
